name: Beth Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, and I lead the bass desk for a small theatre run, teach three advanced pupils, and record guide parts for publishers. My music master’s helps me hear a poor balance quickly, though it does not create another employer in this town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best moment is when the whole band breathes together before a difficult entrance. I use a score checker daily, but I still play what it flags. Helping repair my mother’s roof took almost all our savings, and waiting for a late fee wears me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four of us have an autumn run at the small theatre, and I still record bass lines at home for teaching publishers. I would tell my players that AI Plateau leaves the stage and our fees much as they are. A faster invoice program would be welcome, provided we still check the numbers ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am the best bassist in our little circuit, but there aren't many circuits nearby. Helping repair my mother’s roof emptied our account, and one cancelled theatre week could put the rent behind. A small software saving won't refill that account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the signed theatre dates and the three advanced pupils I coach. Starting with the next extra cleared fee, I will save five percent after rent, other essentials and band wages toward one month of expenses, continuing through this mild change’s first year. I will ask the theatre manager for a written cancellation term before I accept next spring's run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the money, not the playing. A strong bow arm does not turn a cancelled cheque into rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did the roof take from the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost all of the money we had set aside went into my mother’s roof in September. My partner's repair-shop hours help, but they vary from week to week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the theatre offered only a verbal date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the fee and cancellation date in an email before holding the week. An empty calendar is unpleasant; an unpaid reserved week is worse.

say: I would ask for **visible paid calls** while modest software leaves our stage work much the same.
I would welcome a faster **invoice program** if players still check its numbers.
think: Our **thin reserve** makes one lost theatre week a rent problem even if AI mostly stalls.
My **senior playing** gives me work, but there are few nearby employers to replace a cancelled run.
do: Keep **signed theatre dates** and three advanced pupil sessions through the mild first year.
Save **five percent** of extra cleared fees after rent, essentials and band wages toward one month of expenses.
Request a **written cancellation term** before holding next spring's theatre week.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one ordinary cancellation can still upset rent.
fieldNote: Her **public line** trusts live playing, while her rent worry predates the scenario.
The **five-percent transfer** comes only from a fee that has actually cleared.
S0.quote: A strong bow arm does not turn a cancelled cheque into rent.

steps.text: Keep signed theatre dates and three advanced pupil sessions
Save five percent of extra cleared fees after essentials/band wages toward one month
Request written cancellation terms before holding the spring theatre week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At rehearsal I would tell the players that Steady Disruption can make a clean guide track in minutes, but a publisher still has to decide what it will buy. I already use a score checker, which marks possible wrong notes, and I play every marked bar before sending it. I would ask the theatre to keep the human rehearsal fee visible in its contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide recordings pay about a quarter of my own music income, and that part could shrink before anyone replaces a bassist onstage. My playing may remain respected while my invoices get smaller. My partner's repair hours cannot quietly cover that quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will compare my own guide recording with the publisher's licensed new AI guide tool, which drafts practice recordings, checking the notes and keeping pupil files out of it. I will keep the signed theatre run and ask for a separate rehearsal fee in writing. In the first year of the disruption, I will continue the tool only if it saves paid time without losing a client or exposing a pupil's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, though I have enough experience to choose what I send. Losing a quarter of pay would take far longer to repair than a broken string.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a separate rehearsal fee protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre sometimes treats a rehearsal as a favour attached to the show. I would put the rehearsal hours and fee on the same signed sheet as the performance, so the band is paid for both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you know the score checker is safe to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will use only the publisher's licensed file or my own nameless part, and I will play the marked passage against the original score. If a wrong note survives or a pupil's file could leak, the tool stays off that work.

say: I would ask which **guide recordings** publishers will still buy.
I would ask the theatre to keep **human rehearsal fees** visible in contracts.
think: My **guide recordings** could lose buyers while the stage still needs my bass.
Our **household budget** cannot absorb a lasting loss of a quarter of my music income.
do: Compare **licensed AI guide tool** on owned nameless part; check notes/exclude pupils; continue only saving paid time without client loss.
Keep **signed theatre work** and request separate written rehearsal pay in the first disruption year.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing guide fees, though I can test the tool on my own terms.
fieldNote: Her **public confidence** in live bass work does not conceal the vulnerable guide-recording share.
Her **tool trial** is genuine learning on her own or licensed material with manual checks and pupil privacy.
S1.quote: My playing may remain respected while my invoices get smaller.

steps.text: Compare licensed AI guide tool on own part; continue only saving paid time without client loss
Check notes manually, use own nameless music and exclude pupil files; stop errors or leaks
Keep signed theatre work and request separate written rehearsal pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that AGI by 2028 could stop the guide orders before a robot can carry a bass, and the stage robots come about three years later, around 2031. I would ask the publisher what paid human review remains in its new contracts. I would not tell the band that a possible review fee is a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my guide income, roughly a quarter of my music pay, to vanish in 2028. Our reserve is under a month, so that is a real income loss, not a distant argument about robots. A theatre cancellation on top would be worse, but I am not counting it as certain. I lie awake counting the guide fees that would be missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will request the actual pension estimate and keep every signed theatre and pupil date. If the guide orders end in 2028, I will apply only for a posted paid music-director role that accepts my music master's and theatre leadership and pays for human rehearsal direction. In the first year after AGI, I will keep the current paid work until a signed offer gives written take-home pay after travel that replaces the lost guide fees and fits the bus timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the likely guide loss because the account is almost empty already. I can still make calls and keep playing, but that does not make the missing quarter harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for a pension estimate now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 I need the actual figure, not a guess about whether retirement will cover rent. The estimate tells me how much paid playing I may still need at 68; it is not a date I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the theatre for a promising director interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No interview pays rent. I would keep the theatre dates until a qualifying vacancy becomes a signed offer with replacement net pay after travel, and I can actually get there by bus.

say: The **guide orders** could end in 2028, three years before stage robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask publishers for **paid human review** only when it appears in a real contract.
think: I expect a **quarter of music pay** from guides to vanish fast, against almost no reserve.
A lost **theatre run** would deepen the gap, though that second loss is possible rather than expected.
do: Request an **actual pension estimate** and keep signed theatre and pupil work from this month.
Apply after **guide orders end** only for posted director duties accepting my master's and human rehearsal skill.
Keep current paid work until **signed replacement pay** after travel covers lost fees and bus travel fits.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by an expected quarter-income loss against less than a month saved.
fieldNote: The **expected guide loss** supports alarm; further theatre cuts remain a separate uncertainty.
The **director search** requires a qualifying posted vacancy, signed replacement net pay, and workable transport.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed theatre and pupil work
Apply for qualifying posted human rehearsal-director role after guide orders end
Keep current work until signed replacement net pay after travel covers lost fees and bus fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the players that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test a separate live jazz supper, even if guide orders fade earlier. The stage robots are three years later, around 2034, so I will not price 2027 tickets as though a machine has taken our chairs. I would publish the musicians' fees with the ticket offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small concert business could give us income that a publisher cannot delete with one email. Yet a room full of friends who have not paid will not cover the pianist, drummer, venue, or my own playing. Guide money may fade before 2031, so the numbers have to work before the first show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will get written room hire, cancellation and insurance charges, including venue confirmation that the room and equipment are safe for sixty people, before taking ticket money for a separate jazz supper. Sixty prepaid seats must cover the room, required event insurance, both other players, my playing and preparation, and everyone’s travel; otherwise, or if the venue is unsafe, I will defer and refund the whole show. In the first year after 2031 I will renew only on those same written safe full-cost terms and sixty paid seats outside existing theatre dates, keep signed theatre calls, and request my actual pension estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the guide fees, but five years lets me see actual ticket demand. Our jazz supper must cover the band before it puts money in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if fifty-nine people pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If sixty is the break-even number after all costs, fifty-nine is not a green light. I would defer and refund everyone, then ask the venue for a cheaper written room charge before offering another date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the first season use your theatre rehearsal time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the jazz supper would be outside my booked paid theatre calls. I will not trade a signed wage for speculative seats, however flattering the room sounds.

say: I would propose a **separate paid jazz supper** during the five-year warning.
I would publish **musicians’ fees** with the ticket offer.
think: The **guide market** may fade before 2031, so a separate audience could matter.
Unpaid **friendly seats** cannot cover the venue, the band, my preparation, and travel.
do: Get **written venue terms** for sixty safe seats, equipment, hire, cancellation and required insurance charges before ticket payments.
Run only with **sixty prepaid seats** covering room/insurance, band wages, my playing/preparation and everyone’s travel outside paid theatre calls.
Defer and **refund whole show** below paid floor or unsafe; renew after 2031 only on same written safe full-cost terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fading guides, with time to test a fully paid live series.
fieldNote: The **new series** is a distinct producing income stream, not an unpaid extension of existing theatre work.
The **same paid floor** governs launch and renewal; a shortfall refunds the whole group of ticket buyers.
S3.quote: Our jazz supper must cover the band before it puts money in my pocket.

steps.text: Get written safe sixty-seat venue/equipment, hire/cancellation and insurance terms before tickets
Run sixty prepaid seats covering room/insurance, band, own playing/prep, everyone’s travel outside theatre calls
Defer/refund whole show if unsafe or below floor; renew only on same written paid terms
Keep booked theatre calls and request actual pension estimate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our players that AGI by 2036 leaves a decade to protect fees and build the live calendar, but a robot bassist is a later question around 2039. I will still be working at 68 unless the actual pension statement and our accounts say otherwise. The band should keep written terms for every rehearsal and show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is helpful, but our rent is due before any grand technology date. The publishers may stop buying guides well before 2036, and I cannot assume my pension will fill that hole. I could still lead players at 68, yet I need an actual paid calendar rather than a compliment about my reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will request my actual pension estimate and mark the signed theatre and pupil dates through the next season. I will save five percent from each extra cleared fee toward one month of expenses, only after rent, other essentials and band wages are paid. If guide orders end during the decade, I will watch for a posted music-director role accepting my master's and human rehearsal leadership; in the first year after 2036 I will keep current paid work until a signed offer provides replacement take-home pay after travel and a workable bus journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about losing recording money before the date on the card. Ten years before AGI gives me choices, but it does not put an extra month in the bank today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension estimate, our actual rent, and a signed paid calendar would decide it. I would not call retirement funded just because a future robot might play bass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the five-percent saving reliable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a fee that clears can fund that transfer, and I would pay the other musicians first. If the calendar goes quiet, I stop claiming the five percent as savings and protect rent.

say: I would keep **written fees** for rehearsals and shows during the decade of warning.
The **stage-robot date** is around 2039, three years after thinking AGI in 2036.
think: My **guide income** could fade well before 2036, while rent keeps arriving each month.
An **unknown pension** is not a replacement wage just because I will be 68.
do: Request an **actual pension estimate** and keep the signed theatre and pupil calendar.
Save **five percent** of extra cleared fees after essentials and band wages toward one month.
Seek a **posted qualifying director role** if guides end; keep paid work until signed net-after-travel replacement fits buses.
feel: I feel **anxious** because the guide loss may precede AGI and our reserve is still thin.
fieldNote: Her **retirement** remains conditional on an actual pension estimate and paid calendar, with no assumed entitlement.
Her **new-job option** starts only after guide loss and requires a qualifying vacancy, signed replacement pay, and transport.
S4.quote: Ten years before AGI gives me choices, but it does not put an extra month in the bank today.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed theatre and pupil work
Save five percent of extra cleared fees after essentials/band wages toward one month
Apply if guides end for posted director job accepting music master’s and human leadership
Keep paid work until signed net pay after travel replaces fees and bus journey fits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide orders could end before I have rebuilt even one month of rent money. A real posted director opening, written replacement pay after travel, and a pension estimate would give me facts to work with. I would keep my theatre calls until the offer was signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who pays the drummer when a concert is cancelled. A promise to the band is not a wage, and I have had to explain that to more than one venue.

headlineQuote: A promise to the band is not a wage, and I have had to explain that to more than one venue.
portrait: Beth is a **58-year-old** senior bassist with a music master’s, leading theatre players, coaching three pupils, and recording guides.
A roof repair left **less than a month** saved, while her partner’s repair-shop hours vary.
She uses a **score checker** daily but trusts her ear and written pay terms for professional work.
She tests a separately funded **live supper series** only when ticket money covers every worker and cost.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end guide orders before her rent reserve is rebuilt.
whatWouldHelp: A qualifying **paid director vacancy**, signed replacement net pay after travel, and an actual pension estimate would give her options.
